verdict_reasoning: Demand is shown and no surviving objection is fatal, so levels 1a and 1b pass. Level 2 fails on fixable points that the list must settle before code review: replication-ondisk-1 (one compression history across all roles' WAL), maintenance-fit-2 and standards-compat-1 (first protocol extension and client option fixed before the planned codecs, levels and per-direction control have a shape), and replication-ondisk-2 (pooler contract). The author's three design questions in message #1 have no answer yet.

brief.title: Zstandard compression of DataRow and CopyData via negotiated protocol extension
brief.problem: Bulk data such as query results, COPY, pg_restore, base backup and WAL streaming uses a lot of network traffic, which slows clients on limited links. Three earlier protocol compression attempts stalled on negotiation, I/O layering, codec choice, poolers and compression before encryption. This proposal tries a design that answers those questions.
brief.proposed_design: Client and server negotiate _pq_.compression=zstd, and compression starts after the first ReadyForQuery. Server DataRow and CopyData, and client CopyData during COPY FROM, travel as flushed segments of one persistent Zstandard stream per direction inside new CompressedData messages, with a 64 KiB history. Queries, bind parameters and control messages stay uncompressed, and each stream ends before ReadyForQuery or CopyDone/CopyFail so poolers keep their boundaries.
user_visible_surface: New protocol extension _pq_.compression with value zstd, the first defined protocol extension.
New protocol message CompressedData, Byte1('z'), sent by frontend and backend, with 17 MiB payload and 16 MiB output limits.
New server GUC protocol_compression = off | zstd, default off; reload affects only new connections.
New libpq connection option compression = off | prefer | zstd, and environment variable PGCOMPRESSION.
libpq trace output changes (fe-trace.c is touched); the material does not show how.
author_claims: pg_restore client-to-server traffic fell from 264 MB to 21 MB, with median local restore time 3.00 s versus 3.04 s.
Earlier prototype runs cut mixed DataRow and COPY TO traffic to about 10% and 14% of the original size.
One-row pgbench showed no loss (7034 versus 7018 TPS); random data only shrank to about 80% and cost about 0.5 s more CPU.
A 64 KiB history keeps about 1 MiB extra memory per active backend, against about 8.6 MiB with an 8 MiB window.
A pooler can route queries and relay CompressedData without understanding Zstandard; new libpq with prefer connects to an unmodified Postgres 14 server.
brief.thread_state: Jochen Bandhauer shared a measurement script and results showing large traffic cuts and faster runs on LAN and rate-limited links; the author thanked him. Nobody has answered the author's three design questions on message scope, stream boundaries and the policy interface, and CFbot reports the patch needs a rebase.
unclear: The proposal does not say how the server decides that a small result stays uncompressed, or whether users can tune that threshold.
The proposal does not say how a pooler that does not know the extension handles _pq_.compression or CompressedData from a client.
The proposal does not say whether replication connections and pg_basebackup use the compression option, though walsender.c is touched.
The proposal does not say how much decompression memory the server or client keeps per connection.
The material does not say whether compression level or the threshold for skipping compression can be set.
Jochen's results show a 550-fold reduction on an unnamed dataset; the material does not say what data he used.

objections.title: Replication streams share one compression history across all users' WAL
objections.failure_scenario: An administrator sets protocol_compression = zstd, and a standby uses compression=prefer in primary_conninfo over TLS. A low-privilege user on the primary inserts chosen values next to a secret column in another role's table, then watches the replication link. Compressed CopyData lengths over the long-lived walsender stream leak whether the guesses match recent WAL content.
objections.argument: Message #1 names WAL streaming and base backup as covered, and walsender.c is touched. The only reset point is ReadyForQuery, and a START_REPLICATION session can run for days without one. One 64 KiB history then mixes WAL from every database and role. The libpq warning speaks of values in "the same compressed response", and the per-server switch in message #1 does not separate replication connections from ordinary ones.
objections.author_must_show: Do replication and base backup connections use compression, and if so, what bounds history sharing across roles in a walsender stream, or how is it disabled separately?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 lists WAL streaming as covered, and the protocol text allows one backend frame until ReadyForQuery. The 64 KiB history and the two opt-ins narrow the exposure, but the libpq warning does not cover data mixed across roles.

objections.title: First protocol extension fixes scope while the scope question is open
objections.failure_scenario: Drivers and poolers implement _pq_.compression=zstd with the v1 rules: backend DataRow and CopyData, frontend CopyData only, frames that end at ReadyForQuery. A later release wants to compress Bind parameters, add levels, or allow per-direction control. It then needs a second extension or new values, and the project keeps both sets of rules on the server and in libpq indefinitely.
objections.argument: Message #1 asks whether the message scope is "future-proof" and defers levels, more codecs and per-direction control to follow-ups. The documentation hunk defines exact limits and frame rules that become part of the documented protocol. Message #1 says the framing need not change, but the scope and boundary rules are what external implementations will copy. Per-direction control was the UI point that blocked [P4].
objections.author_must_show: How would per-direction control, compression levels and a wider message scope be negotiated later without a second set of rules that servers and libpq must keep?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 says the framing stays, but it does not show how a wider scope, levels or per-direction control would be negotiated under _pq_.compression. [P4] stalled on option syntax, so it supports only the per-direction point.

objections.title: Client option mixes policy and codec, with no room for more codecs
objections.failure_scenario: A later release adds lz4 and compression levels, as message #1 plans. A user who wants "lz4 or zstd, whichever the server allows", or wants zstd at a set level, cannot say so with off | prefer | zstd. libpq then needs a second syntax while connection strings written for the first one stay in use.
objections.argument: Message #1 says new codecs and levels need no framing change, but the client option does change: "prefer" silently means zstd, and a method name means "required". Postgres already separates policy from detail elsewhere: sslmode and sslnegotiation, and pg_dump and pg_basebackup use method[:detail] specs. A committer would likely ask for the full future syntax before the first release, because [P4] stalled on exactly this kind of unclear compression UI.
objections.author_must_show: What connection string will a user write to request lz4-or-zstd at a given level, and does today's syntax extend to it without changing meaning?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 plans more codecs and levels but shows no option syntax for them, and its question 3 on this interface is unanswered. [P4] concerned a different syntax, so it supports only the general point that compression UI gets close review.

objections.title: Transaction poolers must match compression state per server connection
objections.failure_scenario: A transaction-mode pooler forwards a client's _pq_.compression=zstd when it opens a server connection. It later gives that server connection to a client that did not negotiate compression. That client receives a 'z' message in the middle of a result and drops the connection with a protocol error. The user sees this only under load, when the pool mixes clients.
objections.argument: Message #1 says a pooler that passes the negotiation through can relay CompressedData without understanding Zstandard. Negotiation is per server connection, but a transaction pooler shares server connections between clients. To relay safely, the pooler must understand the extension and keep separate pools, or it must decompress. As the first defined protocol extension, this sets the pattern for later ones, so the pooler contract matters beyond this feature.
objections.author_must_show: What must a transaction-mode pooler do with _pq_.compression and CompressedData when its server connections are shared by clients with different settings?

critic.reasoning: The scenario needs a pooler that forwards the extension to a shared server connection, which a pooler that does not know the extension is unlikely to do. But message #1 does not say that relaying requires pooling by negotiated state, and question 2 asks about this.

objections.title: prefer fallback is shown only against a server, not against poolers
objections.failure_scenario: An administrator sets PGCOMPRESSION=prefer for all clients. Some clients connect through an older pooler or proxy that answers an unknown _pq_ startup parameter with a FATAL error rather than NegotiateProtocolVersion. Those clients cannot connect at all, and the cause is not obvious.
objections.argument: _pq_.compression is the first protocol extension that is ever defined, so no middleware has seen one in production. Message #1 reports a fallback test only against an unmodified Postgres 14 server. It says a pooler can relay CompressedData, but it does not say how a pooler that does not know the extension handles the startup parameter. The brief lists this as unclear.
objections.author_must_show: How do common poolers and proxies react today to an unknown _pq_ startup parameter, and does prefer fall back cleanly when one of them rejects it?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 reports the prefer fallback only against a Postgres 14 server. Some pooler versions reject unknown startup parameters with an error, and the proposal does not say whether prefer retries without the extension in that case.

other_surviving.title: No way to see whether a connection negotiated compression
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A DBA sets compression=prefer on a slow link and sees no speedup. psql \conninfo, libpq and pg_stat_* give no sign of whether the server accepted the extension. The DBA cannot tell a disabled server GUC, a pooler that stripped the parameter, and data that compresses poorly apart.
other_surviving.argument: Message #1 leaves pg_stat_* reporting to a follow-up. It names no libpq function and no psql output that shows the negotiated state. SSL and GSS encryption already expose this through libpq functions, psql \conninfo and pg_stat_ssl / pg_stat_gssapi. A silent "prefer" mode with no inspection point departs from that pattern.
other_surviving.author_must_show: Which libpq call and which psql or server view shows a user that a given connection is compressing, in the first release?

critic.reasoning: Message #1 defers pg_stat_* reporting and names no libpq function or psql output for the negotiated state. Deferral does not answer the objection, because prefer falls back silently and SSL and GSS expose their state.

other_surviving.title: Server switch is all-or-nothing, with no per-role, database or pg_hba control
other_surviving.failure_scenario: An admin enables protocol_compression to speed up nightly pg_restore. Every role and database on the cluster can now negotiate compression, including a web application whose results mix user input with session tokens. The admin cannot allow restore traffic and deny the application connections.
other_surviving.argument: Message #1 names the server GUC as the main guard against length leaks, but the docs describe one cluster-wide value with reload semantics. Encryption policy in Postgres can be scoped per host line in pg_hba.conf (hostssl, hostgssenc), and this policy cannot. With PGCOMPRESSION=prefer in a shared environment, any libpq program can opt in without its own decision.
other_surviving.author_must_show: How would an administrator allow compression for restore or backup connections while denying it for a given role, database or pg_hba entry?

critic.reasoning: The client option defaults to off, so the web application compresses only if its own configuration asks. But message #1 presents the server GUC as the administrator's control, and the documentation shows only one cluster-wide value.

refuted.title: Client option repeats the codec-and-policy grammar that blocked [P4]
refuted.failure_scenario: A release ships compression=zstd as the way to require compression, and users put PGCOMPRESSION=zstd into service files. The next release adds lz4, levels and per-direction control, all planned in message #1. It then needs a list or key:value syntax beside the shipped values, which is the syntax [P4] stalled on.
refuted.argument: In [P4] a committer called the libpq_compression syntax a blocker, and a client_to_server/server_to_client form was still under discussion when the entry closed. The new option mixes policy and method in one value: prefer means any codec, zstd means require zstd. Message #1 says codecs, levels and per-direction control need no framing change, but it does not show the interface for them. Message #1 asks question 3 about this interface, and nobody has answered it.
refuted.author_must_show: What will the compression option and protocol_compression GUC look like once lz4, levels and per-direction control exist, and do the v1 values stay valid?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1, which states the same client option concern with a more concrete case.

refuted.title: WAL streaming shares one compression history across all users' changes
refuted.failure_scenario: An admin turns on zstd for a standby that replicates over an observable network. A tenant with insert rights writes guessed values in a loop while other sessions write secrets, and watches the compressed segment sizes. The tenant learns other users' data that RLS or privileges hide, and nobody notices.
refuted.argument: Message #1 says CopyData covers WAL streaming, and walsender.c is touched. In streaming replication, ReadyForQuery does not arrive for a long time, so one stream holds WAL from every session. The libpq warning covers only "the same compressed response" to one application, and does not cover data mixed across users. The server GUC cannot exclude replication.
refuted.author_must_show: Does the walsender compress physical or logical streams, and if so, how does the design stop one role's writes from probing other roles' data through compressed lengths?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of replication-ondisk-1, which describes the same walsender history sharing more precisely.

refuted.title: No committer engaged on a protocol change spanning backend and libpq
refuted.failure_scenario: After commit, a pooler or driver author reports a decoding failure at a frame boundary, or a decompression limit bug on the server. The fix needs someone who knows pqcomm.c, fe-protocol3.c, walsender.c and zstd streaming. If no such committer took part in the design, the report waits while the new protocol rules are already on released servers and clients.
refuted.argument: The thread has three messages: the proposal, one measurement report from a tester (message #2), and a thank-you (message #3). Nobody has answered the three design questions in message #1, and CFbot reports the patch needs a rebase. Earlier attempts closed as returned or withdrawn without a committer taking ownership of the design [P1][P3][P4]. A protocol extension is a long commitment, so a committer would likely ask who signs for it.
refuted.author_must_show: Which committer familiar with the wire protocol and libpq has reviewed the framing rules and is willing to own the protocol extension after commit?

critic.reasoning: A missing committer is a committability note that applies to any ten-week-old thread, and the rubric says it must not raise the verdict. [P1], [P3] and [P4] closed for author inactivity, and a committer was engaged in [P4].

refuted.title: Silent fallback in prefer with no way to see compression state
refuted.failure_scenario: An operator sets compression=prefer in a service file. One client host has a libpq built without Zstandard, where prefer acts as off, so that host gets no compression. Because pg_stat reporting is deferred, the operator cannot see which connections use compression and finds out only from bandwidth bills or slow restores.
refuted.argument: The libpq documentation hunk says prefer is equivalent to off when libpq lacks Zstandard, and message #1 leaves reporting through pg_stat_* to a follow-up. Distribution packages differ in their build options. Shipping the feature before reporting means support questions about whether it works have no answer from the server side.
refuted.author_must_show: How can an administrator or user check, in the first release, whether a given connection negotiated compression and how many bytes it saved?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-3, which covers the same missing way to see whether a connection negotiated compression.

refuted.title: Base backup compression duplicates pg_basebackup's existing server-side compression
refuted.failure_scenario: An administrator runs pg_basebackup --compress=server-zstd over a connection that negotiated _pq_.compression=zstd. The server compresses the tar stream, then compresses the resulting CopyData again. On such near-random input the author's own test shows about 80% size and extra CPU, so the second pass costs CPU for almost no saving.
refuted.argument: Message #1 lists base backup as a beneficiary, and the commit message tests incremental backup. Postgres already compresses base backup traffic on the wire through pg_basebackup --compress=server-gzip|lz4|zstd. The proposal does not say how the two mechanisms interact, or whether walsender skips protocol compression when the backup stream is already compressed. A committer would likely ask for one documented way to compress base backups, not two that stack.
refuted.author_must_show: How does protocol compression behave when pg_basebackup already uses server-side compression, and should replication connections skip it then?

critic.reasoning: Both settings are off by default, so the double compression happens only when a user enables both, and the result is extra CPU with correct output. Server-side backup compression does not cover queries, COPY or WAL streaming, so the mechanisms are not duplicates.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: walsender.c is touched, and message #1 lists base backup and WAL streaming as covered by backend CopyData compression.

touch_points.label: wire protocol
touch_points.reason: The patch defines the first protocol extension, _pq_.compression, and a new CompressedData message, Byte1('z').

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: libpq gains a compression connection option and PGCOMPRESSION, and third-party drivers and poolers must implement the new message to take part.

touch_points.label: new GUC
touch_points.reason: New server GUC protocol_compression = off | zstd, default off.

touch_points.label: psql UX conventions
touch_points.reason: psql gets compression through the libpq option, but the proposal names no \conninfo output or libpq call for the negotiated state.

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: Compression happens before SSL or GSS encryption, so compressed lengths can leak data; the only server control is one cluster-wide GUC.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: New libpq with prefer must connect to older servers and poolers; message #1 tests this only against a Postgres 14 server.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The documented frame rules, size limits and boundary rules become protocol that the server, libpq, drivers and poolers must keep.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: The patch touches pqcomm.c, postgres.c and fe-protocol3.c on the message send and receive paths; default is off.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Do replication and base backup connections use compression, and if so, what bounds history sharing across roles in a walsender stream that never reaches ReadyForQuery?
How will more codecs, compression levels, per-direction control and a wider message scope be negotiated under _pq_.compression without a second set of rules?
What connection string will a user write for lz4-or-zstd at a given level, and do off | prefer | zstd keep their meaning then?
What must a transaction-mode pooler do with _pq_.compression and CompressedData when clients with different settings share its server connections?
Does prefer retry without the extension when a pooler or proxy rejects the unknown _pq_ startup parameter with a FATAL error?

committability.owner_note: It needs a committer who knows the wire protocol, libpq and the walsender; the visible thread has only the author and one tester.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the first protocol extension and a new message type that drivers and poolers will copy, plus the compress-before-encrypt exposure, for as long as protocol 3 lives.
committability.author_follow_up: The author replied to the tester within three days and moved the entry to the next CommitFest, but the rebase that CFbot asked for on 2026-09-02 is not posted.

priority.reason: Four earlier entries since 2018 and the measurements in message #2 show lasting demand from users on slow or metered links. An 88 KiB patch across backend, walsender and libpq adds permanent protocol rules, and the scope, pooler and interface questions are still open.

provisional_note: Without the code I could not check where compression sits relative to secure_read and secure_write, how the walsender uses it, or the threshold for leaving small results uncompressed. The cost for connections that do not negotiate compression is also unchecked.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Libpq Compression
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch series adds protocol-level compression to the wire protocol, on top of a new layered IO stream abstraction that replaces secure_read and secure_write. Client and server announce supported algorithms through the `_pq_.libpq_compression` startup option and a `ParameterStatus` message, and each side then compresses in either direction without further negotiation.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the patch after five months without updates, while waiting for the separate discussion on a protocol message to change GUCs. Robert Haas said the user interface was not clear enough to review, citing `libpq_compression=gzip:compress=off` as confusing. He called these UI questions blockers. A reworked syntax with `client_to_server`/`server_to_client` was being discussed when the entry closed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I would really like to see this patch go forward, but IMHO these UI questions are blockers.

precedents_retrieved.title: Use "protocol options" name instead of "protocol extensions" everywhere
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Heikki Linnakangas, Robert Haas, Jacob Champion, Laurenz Albe, Peter Eisentraut
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch replaces the term "protocol extensions" with "protocol options" in the docs and in a libpq error message, because "extension" suggests a link to Postgres extensions. No protocol options existed yet, so the author saw this as the time to settle on one name.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers did not agree on a new name. Heikki Linnakangas said "protocol option" suggests GUCs, Robert Haas found "protocol extensions" mildly clearer, Jacob Champion preferred keeping "protocol extension" with a docs note, and Laurenz Albe voted to keep "extension" because "option" already names other things in the docs. Peter Eisentraut rejected the patch for lack of consensus to change.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I don't think there is consensus for change, so I'm rejecting it.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add new protocol message to change GUCs to be able to change protocol extension parameters
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a protocol message that lets a client set a GUC without a SET command, so poolers can see the change and some parameters can be set only at the protocol level. Over time the work became a patch set with a protocol minor version bump, min_protocol_version and max_protocol_version libpq options, and protocol parameters such as report_parameters.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the entry and moved the remaining protocol patches to the thread about longer cancel keys. Some pieces were committed here, including a libpq function PQfullProtocolVersion added in place of redefining PQprotocolVersion. The visible messages show no objection that rejected the core design.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: This required another rebase, but I've decided that I think it'll be most fruitful to continue the discussion on protocol changes in the thread about longer cancel keys[1].

precedents_retrieved.title: libpq compression
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds streaming compression of libpq traffic with zlib or zstd, chosen at build time and enabled by a compression connection option, as a replacement for deprecated SSL compression. A compression layer wraps the socket read and write calls in both backend and frontend and passes tx/rx functions into the compression stream.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers objected to the design: the compression option sent in the startup packet, and the compression stream bypassing secure_read()/pqsecure_read() rather than working as a layer under them, which they found invasive. The author and reviewers did not reach consensus on this layering, and Dmitry Dolgov posted an alternative experimental patch. In the last commitfest the patch had failing tests and no review, and the visible messages do not show a closing statement.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I have not actually looked much at your patch, but I am wondering if it could not be possible to make the whole footprint less invasive which really worries me as now shaped.

precedents_retrieved.title: Hooks and API to allow loadable wire protocol extensions
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add hooks and an API so a loadable extension, listed in shared_preload_libraries, can make the postmaster listen on extra ports and serve a different wire protocol, such as TDS. Extensions register callbacks for accept, authentication, error reporting and the TCOP loop, and the existing backend libpq code registers itself through the same API.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show the closing decision; the thread goes silent in March 2021 and the entry was returned in October. The last review objection shown is that the patch's abstractions are still tied to the libpq protocol (cancel key, ready-for-query, simple and extended query), so an extension could not implement another vendor's protocol through them. The author replied that TDS needs a full replacement of PostgresMain(), and that code was not yet posted.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I think, the way the abstractions are chosen in this patch, it is still very much tied to how the libpq protocol works.

precedents_retrieved.title: automatic client-side column-level encryption
precedents_retrieved.summary: Columns marked as encrypted are encrypted and decrypted by the client (libpq), so the server only stores ciphertext in new pg_encrypted_* types. Column encryption keys are catalog objects wrapped by client-held column master keys and sent to clients through new protocol messages behind a _pq_.column_encryption extension.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No closing message is shown, so the visible messages do not state the final reason. The patch stalled in 2023 after extra pg_attribute columns caused a measurable printtup slowdown. After the 2024 rebase, Jelte Fennema-Nio objected that a column encryption key cannot be rotated online, and Robert Haas questioned adding encryption fields to RowDescription and ParameterDescription for every column. The thread ends with no author reply to these points.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: So, I feel quite strongly that shipping the proposed feature without being able to re-encrypt columns in an online fashion would be a mistake.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Reduce checkpoints and WAL traffic on low activity database server"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Reduce checkpoints and WAL traffic on low activity database server"
Reverted commit(s): Reduce checkpoints and WAL traffic on low activity database server Previously, we skipped a checkpoint if no WAL had been written since last checkpoint, though this does not appear in user documentation. As of now, we skip a checkpoint until we have written at least one enough WAL to switch the next WAL file. This greatly reduces the level of activity and number of WAL messages generated by a very low activity server. This is safe because the purpose of a checkpoint is to act as a starting place for a recovery, in case of crash. This patch maintains minimal WAL volume for replay in case of crash, thus maintaining very low crash recovery time.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 18fb9d8d21a28caddb72c7ffbdd7b96d52ff9724.  Per
discussion, it does not seem like a good idea to allow committed changes to
go un-checkpointed indefinitely, as could happen in a low-traffic server;
that makes us entirely reliant on the WAL stream with no redundancy that
might aid data recovery in case of disk failure.

This re-introduces the original problem of hot-standby setups generating a
small continuing stream of WAL traffic even when idle, but there are other
ways to address that without compromising crash recovery, so we'll revisit
that issue in a future release cycle.

roaster_notes.note: The other recorded reasons are inactivity in [P1] and [P3], layering in [P7], and default-off security in [P3]. Each is either answered by this design or does not bear on it. The patch has needed a rebase since 2026-09-02, which is a committability point, not an objection to the idea.
Not applicable. Checks that need the code: the trace output format, how replication connections use the option, and whether 'z' collides with any type byte.
The proposal has no on-disk, WAL format or catalog change, so pg_upgrade and standby replay are not affected; the objections cover only the wire protocol and replication connections.
Decompression memory per segment is bounded and the default is off, so no denial-of-service objection is raised. Earlier requests for an off default appear to be met.
Not applicable. Hot-path cost for non-users looks small with the default off, but this cannot be checked without the code.

No existing feature covers query results, COPY or pg_restore traffic on the wire. An ssh -C tunnel does, but it needs shell access that managed services do not give, and sslcompression was removed, so I raise no general already-exists objection.

The material shows real and lasting demand. Separate authors have tried protocol compression since 2018 ([P7], [P1], [P3], [P4]), and none of those entries ended because nobody wanted it; the recorded reasons are stalled authors, layering and the user interface. In message #2 an independent tester measured large traffic cuts and faster runs on LAN and rate-limited links. The feature is off by default, so its runtime cost falls mainly on the users who turn it on. Design, security and maintenance concerns belong to other angles.
